results.result: SnFR-γ2 and SnFR-γ8 chimeras were successfully engineered by fusing iGluSnFR to auxiliary proteins Stargazin (γ-2) and γ-8. These chimeras showed similar performance to iGluSnFR in HEK cells, associated normally with AMPA receptor complexes, modulated receptor gating, and had similar glutamate affinity to iGluSnFR.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C5 and C23-C27 are well-supported by patch-clamp fluorometry data (Figure 1) showing functional properties, electrophysiology data demonstrating AMPA receptor association and modulation, and concentration-response relationships confirming similar affinity to iGluSnFR. The data provide converging evidence for successful chimera engineering.

results.result: SnFR-γ2 and SnFR-γ8 showed weak enrichment at synapses in hippocampal neurons. Immunocytochemistry revealed about 50% greater average intensity in PSD95-positive spots compared to iGluSnFR, though PSD size was slightly reduced for SnFR-γ2 and the number of PSD spots remained similar across conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C35 are supported by immunocytochemistry data (Figure 3) quantifying surface GFP intensity at PSD95 puncta, PSD area measurements, and puncta counts. The statistical significance (p = 0.03 for SnFR-γ2) and consistent observations across multiple measures support the conclusion of weak synaptic enrichment.

results.result: SnFR-γ2 and SnFR-γ8 showed improved spatial resolution compared to iGluSnFR in spontaneous neurotransmission. The targeted sensors produced more localized signals with half-widths less than 500 nm (approaching diffraction limit at ~300 nm), about three-fold narrower than iGluSnFR, with slightly increased normalized fluorescence amplitudes.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C30 and C36-C39, C41 are supported by fluorescence imaging data (Figures 2, 4) showing distinct spatial patterns, heat map analysis, line profile measurements with Gaussian fitting, and quantification of fluorescence changes. The convergence of multiple spatial analysis methods provides strong evidence for improved spatial resolution.

results.result: Early Stargazin overexpression (before DIV 3) caused a specific postsynaptic deficit in autaptic neurons, resulting in synapses with normal glutamate release but absent or reduced postsynaptic responses. This deficit was reverted by delaying infection to DIV 6, revealing a previously unrecognized developmental pathology.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C8 and C42-C51 are supported by electrophysiology data (Figure 5) showing reduced EPSCs with early infection but normal fluorescence responses, immunocytochemistry showing normal VGLUT puncta, and recovery of EPSCs with late infection. The convergence of optical and electrical measurements, along with the timing-dependent effect, strongly supports this developmental pathology.

results.result: In autaptic neurons, SnFR-γ2 produced more spatially confined signals than iGluSnFR during evoked transmission. Automatically detected ROIs were much smaller for SnFR-γ2 (mean 2.5 μm²) than iGluSnFR (9.6 μm²), with lower correlation between neighboring ROIs, though iGluSnFR produced about twice as many ROIs per neuron.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C56 are supported by fluorescence imaging data (Figures 6, 7) showing spatial patterns, correlation analysis of paired ROI time series, and automated ROI size analysis. The quantitative measurements and statistical comparisons provide strong evidence for improved spatial confinement with SnFR-γ2.

results.result: iGluSnFR showed intense rundown in about half of responsive ROIs during repeated stimulation, while less than 5-7% of SnFR-γ2 ROIs showed similar rundown. Baseline fluorescence remained stable for both sensors, arguing against photobleaching as the primary cause of rundown.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C12 and C57-C61 are supported by analysis of peak responses over 50 stimuli (Figure 7—figure supplement 1) and baseline fluorescence stability measurements (Figure 7—figure supplement 2). The quantitative comparison and stable baseline measurements provide strong evidence for differential rundown behavior.

results.result: SnFR-γ2 is a linear reporter of global quantal parameters and short-term synaptic plasticity, whereas iGluSnFR is not. SnFR-γ2 depression showed excellent correlation with postsynaptic current depression at 2 and 4 mM calcium, while iGluSnFR showed no correlation.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C10 and C66-C72 are supported by simultaneous electrophysiology and fluorescence imaging (Figure 8) showing correlation analysis between optical and electrical measurements of short-term depression. The calcium-dependent changes and quantitative correlation analysis provide strong evidence for SnFR-γ2 as a linear reporter.

results.result: CV analysis revealed that SnFR-γ2 accurately reported calcium-dependent changes in release probability, with monotonic increases in all 6 cells examined, while iGluSnFR only showed monotonic increases in 2 of 6 cells. The SnFR-γ2 values (N=5, PR=0.4 at 2 mM Ca²⁺) matched previous electrophysiological studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C78 are supported by CV analysis (Figure 8G) showing consistent calcium-dependent changes for SnFR-γ2 and comparison to published electrophysiological data. The consistency across cells and agreement with prior work provide strong validation of the approach.

results.result: Quantal analysis revealed that 80% of SnFR-γ2 ROIs were usable for analysis, showing clearer multiple peaks in amplitude distributions than iGluSnFR. The binomial model provided better fits than the Poisson model for most ROIs, with slightly narrower ranges of quantal parameters for SnFR-γ2.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C83 are supported by histogram analysis (Figure 9) showing amplitude distributions, statistical comparison of binomial vs. Poisson fits using Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests, and comparison of parameter distributions. The quantitative analysis and statistical testing provide strong evidence for improved quantal resolution.

results.result: The Y230F mutation in iGluSnFR increased ΔF/F and sped off-kinetics but reduced glutamate affinity. Paradoxically, this low-affinity mutant gave almost no response to evoked release in autaptic neurons despite responding to direct glutamate application, leading to the hypothesis that it was not sufficiently close to synaptic glutamate signals.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C21 are supported by patch-clamp fluorometry data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) showing altered kinetics and affinity, and fluorescence imaging (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) showing lack of evoked responses but normal responses to direct application. The paradoxical behavior provides strong motivation for the synaptic targeting approach.

results.result: EPSC peak amplitude typically reduced by about 40% over 50 stimuli for both sensors. The iGluSnFR rundown exaggerated current rundown while SnFR-γ2 possibly underestimated it, consistent with iGluSnFR preferentially reporting spillover glutamate.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C65 are partially supported by EPSC rundown analysis (Figure 7—figure supplement 2), but the interpretation that iGluSnFR reports spillover (C65) is speculative. The differential rundown patterns are documented, but the mechanistic explanation requires additional validation.

results.result: Inline fusion of iGluSnFR into AMPA receptor subunits GluA1 and GluA2 produced sensors with very small ΔF/F.
results.evaluation: Claim C22 is supported by patch-clamp fluorometry data (Figure 1—figure supplement 3) showing weak fluorescence responses for GluA2/A1 SnFR chimeras. This negative result motivated the alternative TARP-based targeting strategy.

results.result: SnFR-γ2 gave similar quantal parameters from CV analysis to previous electrophysiological work (N=5, PR=0.4), suggesting it is a fair reporter of presynaptic release and that postsynaptic short-term plasticity is limited at frequencies up to 5 Hz.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C85 are supported by CV analysis results (Figure 8) and comparison to published electrophysiological data. The agreement with prior work and correlation with simultaneous electrical measurements provide strong validation.

results.result: Optical glutamate measurement eliminates postsynaptic receptors as a variability source. The authors saw little evidence for vesicular glutamate content variation as a major source of variability, contrary to previous simulations. AMPA receptors have lower glutamate affinity than SnFR-γ2 and are probably often not saturated.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C91 mix supported observations (C86, C90 based on known receptor properties) with inferences from data (C88 based on invariant quantal sizes) and speculative explanations (C89, C91). The interpretation requires additional experimental validation to distinguish between sensor saturation and true biological invariance.

results.result: Confining iGluSnFR to presynaptic terminals gives quantal amplitude distributions, and changing calcium concentration while examining the same terminal is beneficial for determining quantal parameters.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C93 are supported by citations to previous work and confirmed by the current experimental approach. The consistency with prior studies and successful application in the current work provide validation.

results.result: The authors propose that iGluSnFR rundown may result from bleaching being more intense when glutamate is bound, with iGluSnFR having greater average glutamate occupancy than SnFR-γ2. SnFR-γ2 would be protected by seeing only fast transients that immediately disperse.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C96 are entirely speculative mechanistic explanations for the observed rundown phenomenon. While the hypothesis is plausible and illustrated in Figure 10, no direct experimental evidence is provided to test this mechanism. Additional experiments would be needed to validate this explanation.

results.result: Based on previous diffusion studies and expansion microscopy, the PDGFR motif of iGluSnFR is likely excluded from synapses. The density of SnFR-γ2 must be lower outside synapses than inside, and greater extrasynaptic capacity would bias iGluSnFR against measuring synaptic glutamate.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C100 are supported by citations to previous work on protein diffusion and expansion microscopy, combined with logical inferences about sensor distribution. The consistency with prior studies and the current observations of improved spatial resolution provide support for this interpretation.

results.result: Neither iGluSnFR nor SnFR-γ2 can reliably identify single release events in the experimental conditions used, but for different reasons: iGluSnFR shows intense rundown while SnFR-γ2 has low signal amplitude. However, SnFR-γ2 could resolve spontaneous neurotransmission at spot-like ROIs.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C104 are supported by the rundown analysis (Figure 7—figure supplement 1) and signal-to-noise considerations from the data, along with spontaneous transmission imaging (Figure 2). The limitations are clearly documented and explained.

results.result: The improved spatial profiles of SnFR-γ2 are expected to benefit short-term plasticity studies. However, using mouse auxiliary proteins may not be universal and may influence synaptic transmission undesirably in other systems. Stargazin overexpression suggests a postsynaptic deficit in cultured hippocampal cells, with intact glutamate release and no obvious effects on GABAergic transmission.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C110 are supported by the short-term plasticity data (Figure 8), electrophysiology showing postsynaptic deficits (Figure 5), and observations from inadvertent GABAergic recordings. The cautionary statements about generalizability are appropriate given the system-specific effects observed.

results.result: Sensor performance is always worse in vivo, and the sensor is probably better suited to quantitative studies of synaptic transmission in vitro rather than in vivo work, though performance should not be worse than iGluSnFR.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C112 are supported by general knowledge about sensor performance in different contexts and comparison to recent related work. The recommendation is appropriately cautious and based on the characteristics demonstrated in vitro.

results.result: Stargazin has a very long first intron that is the target of mutations reducing γ-2 mRNA and thought to delay expression. Release and presynaptic VGLUT1 markers were normal despite non-functional synapses with early Stargazin overexpression, suggesting Stargazin is not the ideal host and that uncomplexed auxiliary proteins may fill PSD slots.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C120 are supported by citations to molecular biology literature, electrophysiology and immunocytochemistry data (Figure 5), and logical inferences about the mechanism. The combination of documented effects and mechanistic speculation is appropriately presented.

results.result: SnFR-γ8 performance was similar to SnFR-γ2 but with less broad labeling and fewer responding ROIs, possibly because tethered sensors preferentially select stronger synapses. The NETO2 transmembrane helix appears to reduce expression and is more damaging to synaptic transmission than native Stargazin.
results.evaluation: Claims C121-C124 are supported by fluorescence imaging observations and electrophysiology data comparing different constructs (Figure 5G). The speculation about preferential selection of stronger synapses is appropriately presented as a possibility.

results.result: The targeted sensor did not have distinctly better signal-to-noise than iGluSnFR. A recent report used similar tethering principles. Disadvantages include potential loss of non-synaptic signals and inability to guarantee exclusive measurement of synaptic glutamate. Spectral variants with distinct targeting could provide a fuller picture.
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C129 are supported by the data showing similar noise levels, citations to related work, and logical considerations about the limitations and future directions. The balanced assessment of advantages and limitations is appropriate.

results.result: Various approaches can augment iGluSnFR signal including superfolder GFP, mutagenesis, or different promoters. The superfolder variant was used successfully for quantal analysis when confined to presynaptic sites. Other tethers may give better, more defined, or orthogonal signals.
results.evaluation: Claims C130-C132 are supported by citations to previous work and the current experimental approach. The suggestions for future work are appropriately speculative and based on the current findings.

results.result: SnFR-γ2 and SnFR-γ8 possibly experienced higher saturation than iGluSnFR during spontaneous neurotransmission.
results.evaluation: Claim C40 is purely speculative and offered as a possible explanation for increased normalized fluorescence changes. No direct evidence for saturation is provided, and alternative explanations are not ruled out. This requires additional experimental validation.
